title: The Shower Problem
question: Why can't I just get the shower to 38 °C?

blocks.text: Okay, confession. This morning I turned the shower knob, got **boiled**, turned it back, got **frozen**, and did that about six times.
Everybody does that! Old apartment showers are the worst.
But *why* is it hard? You want one number, 38 degrees. You have one knob. That should be easy.

Let's find out. Below is a shower with a **long pipe** between the knob and the shower head, like a real one. Water you mix at the knob takes a couple of seconds to travel up the pipe. You can watch the water's colour creep along it.

**Your goal:** get the water to {sp|38 °C} (the green band) and keep it there for 10 seconds straight. Drag the {eff|orange knob}, or click it and use the arrow keys. The clock starts when you touch it.
The pipe has a 2.5-second delay. That's about what you get from a few metres of pipe.
How did it go? If you swung back and forth, over and under the green band, you're in good company. Look at the {out|blue curve}: it probably zig-zags like a nervous snake.
I think the shower is broken. I set the knob to *warm*, and it keeps going *hot* anyway!
Hmm. Let's plot two things: what the knob **asks for** and what the head **gives you**. If it's broken they shouldn't match at all.

The {eff|dotted orange curve} is the temperature your knob position *asks for*: the mix at the valve. The {out|blue curve} is what actually arrives. Slide the orange curve later in time and see if they line up.
Oh! Slide it about 3 seconds and they're almost the **same curve**. The shower isn't broken…
…it's just **late**! Everything I felt was about 3 seconds old.

That's the first clue. When you feel "too hot", you're feeling the knob position from a few seconds ago. By then you've *already* turned it hotter, so you turn it back, too far, and the cycle starts again.
2.5 s is the pipe. The extra half-second or so is the water mixing and warming the metal. It smooths out sudden changes.
I've got it: I was too **gentle**! If I turn the knob **faster** whenever it's wrong, I'll fix it faster.

We built three robot hands to test ideas without getting wet. The **normal hand** turns the knob a little faster the more wrong the water feels, like most people do. The **harder hand** does exactly the same thing, twice as vigorously.

blocks.q: Compared with the normal hand, what will the **harder** hand do?

options.why: That's what our gut says: more effort, faster result.

options.text: About the same, only slightly quicker
options.why: A reasonable hedge, but the delay makes things much more dramatic than that.

options.text: Swing even harder and never settle
options.why: Turning faster means that by the time the (late) water tells you to stop, you've turned *even further*. The swings grow until the knob hits its ends.

blocks.text: Try all three. The **harder** hand thrashes between freezing and scalding. The **patient** hand sets the knob to about 51% (the right mix, worked out in advance) and simply *waits*. It wins easily.
So delay alone isn't the problem. The patient hand has the same delay and does fine. The problem is **reacting to old news, too eagerly**.
So "push harder when you're further off" is the *wrong* instinct? That's my whole personality.
But the patient hand cheated. It knew the right answer in advance. If the hot water tank cools down, or someone flushes a toilet, the right knob position changes and the patient hand won't notice.
That's the real puzzle. We need something that **reacts** (so it can handle surprises) but doesn't **over-react** (so it doesn't swing). Hold on to that thought. The whole course is about it.

items: Having a **goal** (38 °C) and a way to act (the knob) isn't enough. **How** you react matters.
A **delay** means you always feel old information. The shower isn't broken, it's late.
Reacting harder to old information makes the swings **worse**, not better.
Setting the knob once and waiting works, but only if nothing ever changes.

items.q: At t = 5 s you snap the knob from cold to warm. Roughly when does the temperature at the head **start** to rise?

options.why: The water you just mixed is still at the bottom of the pipe. The head keeps getting the old cold water for a while.
Right: 2.5 s later, when the new water has travelled the pipe. After that it rises smoothly over about a second as it mixes.
Too late: our pipe's delay is 2.5 s, not 10 s.

items.q: You set the knob exactly right (51%) and walk away. What happens?

options.text: It warms up and settles at 38 °C without swinging
options.why: Yes. Delay only makes things **late**. Swinging comes from *reacting* to late information.

options.text: It swings forever, because of the delay
options.why: Delay by itself doesn't create swings. Nobody is reacting, so nothing can overshoot.
It gets there: 2.5 s of delay, then about a second of smooth warming.

items.q: Which temperature plot belongs to someone who **reacts too hard**?

options.why: Over-reacting to delayed information pumps energy into the swings, like pushing a swing at just the wrong moments.
Shrinking swings mean the reactions are gentle enough to calm down. That's a *gentle* reactor.
That's the patient hand: set it and wait. No over-reaction at all.

blocks.text: A tiny drone hovers perfectly still at 2 metres, in the wind, with no brain at all. It has the same problem we do. **How does it solve it?**
